# Finite subgroups of the profinite completion of good groups

Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul

MB

Marco Boggi

PZ

Pavel Zalesskii

## Abstract

Let $G$G be a residually finite, good group of finite virtual cohomological dimension. We prove that the natural monomorphism $G\hookrightarrow\hat{G}$G↪G^ induces a bijective correspondence between conjugacy classes of finite $p$p-subgroups of $G$G and those of its profinite completion $\hat{G}$G^. Moreover, we prove that the centralizers and normalizers in $\hat{G}$G^ of finite $p$p-subgroups of $G$G are the closures of the respective centralizers and normalizers in $G$G. With somewhat more restrictive hypotheses, we prove the same results for finite solvable subgroups of $G$G. In the last section, we give a few applications of this theorem to hyperelliptic mapping class groups and virtually compact special toral relatively hyperbolic groups (these include fundamental groups of $3$3-orbifolds and of uniform standard arithmetic hyperbolic orbifolds).

### Abstract

Let $$G$$ be a residually finite, good group of finite virtual cohomological dimension. We prove that the natural monomorphism $$G\hookrightarrow {\widehat{G}}$$ induces a bijective correspondence between conjugacy classes of finite $$p$$-subgroups of $$G$$ and those of its profinite completion $${\widehat{G}}$$. Moreover, we prove that the centralizers and normalizers in $${\widehat{G}}$$ of finite $$p$$-subgroups of $$G$$ are the closures of the respective centralizers and normalizers in $$G$$. With somewhat more restrictive hypotheses, we prove the same results for finite solvable subgroups of $$G$$. In the last section, we give a few applications of this theorem to hyperelliptic mapping class groups and virtually compact special toral relatively hyperbolic groups (these include fundamental groups of 3-orbifolds and of uniform standard arithmetic hyperbolic orbifolds).

The main goal of the present article is to achieve (for one particular tower and version of \(\widehat{GT}\)) the converse which was obtained in the genus zero situation, namely to show that the group is not just *an* outer automorphism group of the tower, but *the whole* outer automorphism group. This is something which has proved unexpectedly difficult in higher genus, because it necessitates the computation of centralizers of Dehn twists in the profinite mapping class group. In the genus zero case, only the first two groups \(\widehat{\Gamma}_{0,4}\) and \(\widehat{\Gamma}_{0,5}\) are needed. Grothendieck raised the question for \(\widehat{\Gamma}_{0,4}\), which is the profinite free group on two generators, and noted that he could not see how to solve it (“consulter Deligne à ce sujet”, Récoltes et Semailles). It was proved by Belyi and later by others in more generality. The case of \(\widehat{\Gamma}_{0,5}\) was solved with complete computations of the centralizers of Dehn twists by Nakamura [N, Appendix]. In both cases, the results show that the centralizers of Dehn twists are exactly analogous to those in the discrete mapping class groups. (https://webusers.imj-prg.fr/~leila.schneps/serre80.pdf)

The case of \(\widehat{\Gamma}_{0,5}\) was solved with complete computations of the centralizers of Dehn twists by Nakamura [N, Appendix]. In both cases, the results show that the centralizers of Dehn twists are exactly analogous to those in the discrete mapping class groups.

The key result which has made it possible to show the analogous result in all genera in the present article is due to Marco Boggi [B], whose theorem can be roughly stated as follows (see Theorem 2.1 for a more detailed version). We consider each discrete mapping class group \(\Gamma\) to be identified with its image under the natural inclusion into its profinite completion \(\widehat{\Gamma}\).

**Boggi’s Theorem.** [B] *The centralizer in the profinite mapping class group \(\widehat{\Gamma}\) of a Dehn twist in \(\Gamma\) is isomorphic to the profinite completion of the centralizer in \(\Gamma\).*

In fact, in this article, we only use the weaker statement that the centralizer in \(\widehat{\Gamma}\) of a Dehn twist in \(\Gamma\) is topologically generated by the centralizer of the twist in \(\Gamma\) (i.e. a quotient of the profinite completion).

### Corrigendum to Minimum polynomials and lower bounds for eigenvalue multiplicities of prime-power order elements in representations of classical groups [J. Algebra 243 (2001) 228¿263]

##### DI MARTINO, LINO GIUSEPPE;Zalesskii, AE

##### 2006

#### Abstract

This note is an addendum to the paper “Minimum polynomials and lower bounds for eigenvalue multiplicities of prime-power order elements in representations of classical groups” [J. Algebra 243 (2001) 228–263], providing a correct full statement and proof of Theorem 1.1 in that paper, and thus yielding a complete classification of the triples (G, g, theta), where G is a quasi-simple classical group, g is a semisimple element of G of prime-power order belonging to a parabolic subgroup, and theta is a representation of G in cross-characteristic, in which the degree of the minimum polynomial of g is ‘exceptional’. This result can be viewed as an analogue of the celebrated Hall–Higman theorem in the context of quasi-simple classical groups.

L39: ## 1. Introduction
L40: ### 1.1. The congruence subgroup property
L41: Let $S$ be an oriented connected surface of negative Euler characteristic and finite type and let $G$ be a finite group acting faithfully on $S$. The group $G$ then identifies with a finite subgroup of the mapping class group ${\Gamma}(S)$ of the surface $S$ and let us denote by ${\Gamma}(S)^{G}$ the centralizer of $G$ in ${\Gamma}(S)$. Let $\Pi$ be the fundamental group of $S$ for some choice of base point.
L42: There is a natural faithful representation $\rho_{S}\colon\thinspace{\Gamma}(S)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Out}(\Pi)$ which restricts to a faithful representation $\rho_{S,G}\colon\thinspace{\Gamma}(S)^{G}\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Out}(\Pi)$.
L43: For an abstract group $L$, let us denote by $\widehat{L}$ its profinite completion. The homomorphisms $\rho_{S}$ and $\rho_{S,G}$ then induce the homomorphisms of profinite groups:
L44: 
L45: (1)  |  | $$\hat{\rho}_{S}\colon\thinspace{\widehat{\Gamma}}(S)\to\operatorname{Out}({\widehat{\Pi}})\hskip 28.45274pt\mbox{and}\hskip 28.45274pt\hat{\rho}_{S,G}\colon\thinspace{\widehat{\Gamma}}(S)^{G}\to\operatorname{Out}({\widehat{\Pi}}).$$  |
L46: The congruence subgroup problem for the mapping class group ${\Gamma}(S)$ (resp. for ${\Gamma}(S)^{G}$) asks whether the homomorphism $\hat{\rho}_{S}$ (resp. $\hat{\rho}_{S,G}$) is faithful.
L47: More conventionally, this question can be reformulated by asking whether, for every finite index subgroup ${\Gamma}$ of ${\Gamma}(S)$ (resp. of ${\Gamma}(S)^{G}$), there exists a finite index characteristic subgroup $K$ of $\Pi$ such that the kernel of the induced representation ${\Gamma}(S)\to\operatorname{Out}(\Pi/K)$ (resp. ${\Gamma}(S)^{G}\to\operatorname{Out}(\Pi/K)$) is contained in ${\Gamma}$. The first question is known to have a positive answer for $g(S)\leq 2$ (cf.
L48: [【18†1】], [【19†2】], [【20†6】]), where $g(S)$ denotes the genus of $S$.

Let $R$ and $B$ be, respectively, the ramification and the branch locus of $p_{G}$ and put $S^{\circ}:=S\smallsetminus R$ and $S_{/G}^{\circ}:=S_{/G}\smallsetminus B$. The main result of the paper is then (cf. Theorem 【21†4.1】 for a slightly more general result):

L36: ## 1. Introduction
L37: Let $G$ be a residually finite group, ${\widehat{G}}$ its profinite completion and $\iota\colon\thinspace G\hookrightarrow{\widehat{G}}$ the natural monomorphism. The map $\iota$ induces a map $\iota_{c}$ from the set of conjugacy classes of finite subgroups of $G$ to the set of conjugacy classes of finite subgroups of ${\widehat{G}}$.
L38: A natural question is then whether this map is injective, in which case we say that $\iota$ separates conjugacy classes of finite subgroups, and whether it is surjective, i.e. whether every finite subgroup of ${\widehat{G}}$ is conjugated to a finite subgroup of $\iota(G)$ (from now on, we will simply denote by $G$ the image of $\iota$).
L39: Of course, the question can be formulated for a residually ${\mathscr{C}}$ group $G$ and the pro-${\mathscr{C}}$ completion $G_{\widehat{{\mathscr{C}}}}$ respectively, where ${\mathscr{C}}$ is a class of finite groups closed for subgroups, quotients and extensions. The classes of finite $p$-groups or finite solvable groups are of particular interest. As matter of notation, a ${\mathscr{C}}$-group is a group in ${\mathscr{C}}$.
L40: The problem of whether $\iota_{c}$ is injective is the restriction of the subgroup conjugacy separability problem, namely of whether two distinct conjugacy classes of subgroups of $G$ have distinct images in some finite quotient of $G$, to finite subgroups of $G$. Examples of subgroup conjugacy separable groups are virtually polycyclic groups (cf. [【17†13】]), virtually free groups (cf.
L41: [【18†7】]) and hyperbolic virtually compact special groups (in particular, Fuchsian and one-relator groups with torsion) (cf. [【19†6】]). In particular, for all these groups, the map $\iota_{c}$ is injective.
L42: On the other hand, the problem of whether the map $\iota_{c}$ is surjective has not been much studied. This is true for finitely generated nilpotent groups (since, in this case, torsion elements form a finite normal subgroup), for virtually free groups by [【20†27】, Theorem 3.10] (cf. also [【21†21】, Theorem 1.2]).
L43: Kropholler and Wilson [【22†16】, Theorem 2.7] proved the surjectivity of $\iota_{c}$ for residually finite solvable minimax (in particular, polycyclic) groups and constructed counterexamples for infinitely generated nilpotent groups of class $2$ and for finitely generated center-by-metabelian groups.
L44: In general, the answer is negative and it is not difficult to give some examples. For instance, for $n\geq 2$, there holds $\widehat{\operatorname{Sp}_{2n}({\mathbb{Z}})}\cong\operatorname{Sp}_{2n}(\widehat{\mathbb{Z}})$ (cf. [【23†2】]) and the natural homomorphism $\iota\colon\thinspace\operatorname{Sp}_{2n}({\mathbb{Z}})\to\operatorname{Sp}_{2n}(\widehat{\mathbb{Z}})$ is injective.
L45: However, the center of $\operatorname{Sp}_{2n}({\mathbb{Z}})$ consists of the scalar matrices $\pm{\mathrm{I}}$ and is a finite subgroup of order $2$, while the center of $\operatorname{Sp}_{2n}(\widehat{\mathbb{Z}})\cong\prod_{p}\operatorname{Sp}_{2n}({\mathbb{Z}}_{p})$ contains elementary abelian $2$-subgroups of any order. Thus $\iota_{c}$ in this case is not surjective. In fact, this is the case for any arithmetic group for which the congruence subgroup problem has a positive solution.
L46: The reason for which the linear group $\operatorname{Sp}_{2n}({\mathbb{Z}})$ and, in general, arithmetic groups with a positive solution to the congruence subgroup problem fail to satisfy the desired property is that these groups are not good (cf. [【24†12】, Proposition 5.1 and Remark 5.3]). Let us recall this notion.
L47: In this paper, for a given profinite group $R$ and prime number $p>0$, the coefficients for the cohomology of $R$ will be in the category of discrete ${\mathbb{F}}_{p}[[R]]$-modules, where ${\mathbb{F}}_{p}[[R]]$ is the completed group algebra of $R$ with ${\mathbb{F}}_{p}$-coefficients. A discrete ${\mathbb{F}}_{p}[[R]]$-module is equivalently described as an ${\mathbb{F}}_{p}$-vector space, with the discrete topology, endowed with a continuous linear action of the profinite group $R$.
